title: Heritability in the genomics era — concepts and misconceptions

claims.statement: In people born from 1950 to 1993 and adopted in Sweden outside their biological family (adoptions by relatives or by a biological parent's partner excluded), with register information on both adoptive parents and at least one biological parent, both what was passed on from their biological parents and features of the adoptive home they grew up in were associated with a later register record of drug problems; the study estimated no heritability percentage. Of 18,115 adoptees followed in national registers to 2009 (a record meant a diagnosis of a drug use disorder or drug psychosis in hospital, outpatient, primary-care or death records; a conviction under two crime-register codes for crimes related to drug abuse, convictions only for alcohol-related crimes or only for drug trafficking or possession not counting; or long-term high-volume collection of prescribed sedatives, hypnotics or opioids; alcohol and tobacco excluded; the study calls this 'drug abuse'), 4.5% had a record, against 2.9% of everyone in Sweden born in the same years. Adoptees whose biological parent had a record, though they were not raised by that parent, had one in 8.6% of cases against 4.2% when neither biological parent had (odds ratio 2.09, 95% CI 1.66 to 2.62), and in 11.9% when both had; records were also shared with biological siblings raised apart (full siblings, odds ratio 1.84, 1.28 to 2.64; half siblings, 1.41, 1.19 to 1.67). In the adoptive home, records were shared with adoptive siblings, who were not biologically related to the adoptee: 6.2% of the adoptive siblings of adoptees with a record had one, against 3.2% of the adoptive siblings of adoptees without (odds ratio 1.95, 1.43 to 2.65), and the adoptive mother's divorce and an adoptive parent's death were also associated with a record; adoptees raised by an adoptive parent with a record had one in 6.8% of cases against 4.5%, an imprecise estimate that included no difference (1.55, 0.86 to 2.80), with only 1.0% of adoptive parents affected. On the scale of absolute risk, an adverse adoptive home added more risk for adoptees whose biological relatives' records put them at higher risk, an interaction the paper does not report on the odds scale; at the lowest level of the biological-relative index the added risk could not be told apart from none (Kendler et al., 2012). An adoption study separates the family that passes on genes from the family that raises a child, but what passes from biological parents includes the pregnancy, care before placement (up to about 3 in 10 adoptees may have joined their adoptive family after age 5, by a census-based estimate) and how agencies matched children to homes (modest, by the authors' judgment), as well as genes. The authors report that children usually spent the time before placement in a nursery or foster home rather than with their biological parents, and that later placement did not go with a higher risk (odds ratio 0.96 per year before adjustment, 1.00 after); their argument against effects in the womb rests on 9.9% with an affected biological father against 8.2% with an affected mother, overlapping intervals without a test. As summarized, without figures, by a narrative review, twin studies find that genes and both shared and individual environment influence whether people start using tobacco, alcohol or cannabis, that genes matter more for regular use and dependence, and that the environment twins share is no longer detectable for regular use or dependence in adulthood though it is in adolescence (the adoptive-sibling association above, if it reflects the shared home, does not fit this summary well); single genetic variants have small effects that replicate poorly, scores combining many variants explained less than 1% of the variation in alcohol dependence, and the size of genetic influence has been reported to differ between environments (Prom-Wormley et al., 2017, second-hand). A heritability, where one is given, is a ratio: the share of the differences between people in one population, for a trait measured at a particular time or age, that goes with differences in their genes. It is not the share of any one person's risk, or of a trait, that comes from genes; a high heritability does not mean that genes fix the outcome or that the environment cannot change it (human height has a heritability of about 0.8, yet average height has risen over generations); and it says nothing about why groups differ or why levels change over time. Because it depends on how much the genes and the environments vary, it can change when environments change, with age and with how the trait is measured, and in theory a figure from one population does not predict another, though the heritabilities of similar traits are often similar across populations; for a diagnosis, the figure is much smaller on the observed yes-or-no scale than on an assumed underlying scale of liability when the condition is rare; and the classical twin design estimates only three variance components and overstates heritability when identical twins share more of their environment than non-identical twins do, or when genes and environments are correlated (Visscher et al., 2008, a conceptual review by geneticists that discusses no drug-use figure). Certainty: low. Status: single study.
claims.magnitude: Kendler et al. (2012): adoptees with a record 4.5% (95% CI 4.2–4.8; 820 people) vs 2.9% nationally for the same birth years. Biological parent with vs without a record 8.6% vs 4.2%, OR 2.09 (1.66–2.62); none, one or both biological parents 4.2%, 8.2%, 11.9%; biological father 9.9% (7.2–12.1), mother 8.2% (6.3–10.5). Biological full siblings raised apart, record in 10.7% of the full siblings of adoptees with a record vs 6.1% of those of adoptees without, OR 1.84 (1.28–2.64); half siblings 7.4% vs 5.3%, OR 1.41 (1.19–1.67). Adoptive siblings of adoptees with vs without a record 6.2% vs 3.2%, OR 1.95 (1.43–2.65); adoptees raised by an adoptive parent with vs without a record 6.8% vs 4.5%, OR 1.55 (0.86–2.80). Multivariable: adoptive mother's divorce OR 1.31 (1.03–1.68), adoptive parent's death 1.37 (1.08–1.73). Interaction on the probability scale 0.0005 per decile × decile (0.0001–0.0008): each decile of the adoptive-home index added about 0.15 percentage points of risk at the lowest decile of the biological-relative index (the main effect with the interaction term, 0.0015, −0.0006 to 0.0036, an interval that includes no added risk) and about 0.6 at the highest (editors' calculation on the study card, recomputed with deciles coded 0 to 9). Later placement: odds ratio 0.96 per year before adjustment, 1.00 after. No heritability estimated. As summarized by Prom-Wormley et al. (2017): polygenic scores explained less than 1% of the variance in alcohol dependence; no twin heritability figure for any drug use disorder is given.
